issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette:
Frank is a 77-year-old delivery driver, a job he has held for over three decades and which once felt as natural as breathing. The assault that upended his life happened eight months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late November. He had pulled his truck into the loading bay of a large hardware store, a routine stop he had made hundreds of times. As he stepped out of the cab, a man he had never seen before came at him from behind the dumpster, demanding the keys to the truck. Frank, startled but not yet afraid, had tried to calmly explain that he couldn't do that. The man didn't argue. He simply struck Frank across the face with a heavy metal pipe. The pain was immediate and sickening, a bright white light behind his eyes. He remembers the wet, sharp crack of his own cheekbone breaking, and the feeling of his knees hitting the cold asphalt. The man took the keys and drove the truck twenty feet before abandoning it, but for Frank, the world had already ended. He was left on the ground, bleeding, unable to move, waiting for someone to find him.

In the weeks that followed, Frank tried to convince himself it was just a bad moment, a story to tell. He refused to take more than a few days off, insisting he was fine. But the world outside his front door had become a place of hidden threats. Every blind corner on his delivery route, every person standing too still near a loading dock, every unexpected sound from behind a parked car-his body would seize up, his heart hammering against his ribs. He started taking longer routes to avoid the hardware store, and then to avoid any street that looked like the one he was on. He told his wife, Margaret, that he was just being careful, that at his age he had to watch his step. But what he could not tell her was that he had begun to believe something far more frightening: that he could no longer trust his own judgment. He had always prided himself on reading people, on knowing when a situation was safe. But he had walked right into that loading bay. He had not seen the threat coming. Now, every decision felt suspect. He would stand in the grocery aisle for five minutes, paralyzed, because he could not be sure which route to the register was the safe one. He had come to believe that if he let his guard down for even a second, he would be caught off guard again, and this time, he might not get up.

To manage the constant, low-grade dread, Frank worked harder. He volunteered for extra shifts, taking any run that would keep him behind the wheel for ten or twelve hours. The motion of the truck, the focus required to navigate traffic, the sheer exhaustion-these things pushed the memory of the pipe and the asphalt to the edges of his mind. He was grateful for the fatigue, because it meant that when he finally fell into bed, he was too tired to dream. But the strategy had a cost. He was snapping at Margaret, withdrawing from their weekend card games with the neighbors, and eating mechanically, almost unconsciously, at the end of every shift. He would come home, sit in the dark kitchen, and eat an entire loaf of bread or a bag of cookies, not out of hunger, but as a way to fill the hollow, trembling feeling inside him. He knew it was unhealthy, but it was easier than sitting with the thought that had begun to haunt him: that his understanding of the world-a world where hard work and decency kept you safe-had been completely destroyed.

He tried not to think about the assault. He would actively steer his mind away whenever the image of the pipe swinging toward his face surfaced, because he was certain that if he let himself really think about it, he would not be able to handle it. The memory would swallow him whole. He would be back on that cold ground, helpless, and he was terrified that he might never find his way out again. It was Margaret who finally convinced him to seek help. He had come home one evening, exhausted and hollow-eyed, and she had simply said, "Frank, you're not here anymore. You left the day that man hit you." He had no argument. What frightened him most now was not the memory of the assault itself, but the growing certainty that the man he used to be-the confident, decisive driver who knew the city like the back of his hand-was gone for good, and he did not know how to find his way back.
